bib.title: Is Cosine-Similarity of Embeddings Really About Similarity?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Is Cosine-Similarity of Embeddings Really About Similarity?", Harald Steck, Chaitanya Ekanadham, Nathan Kallus (Netflix; Kallus also Cornell), arXiv:2403.05440v1 [cs.IR], 8 Mar 2024 (dated March 11, 2024). Preprint, 9 pages.

COVERAGE: 21338 of 21338 chars read (all pages, including references). Nothing skipped. Figure 1 image not viewed; only its caption was extracted from the text. Equations are garbled in places (see PROBLEMS).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Cosine similarity of learned embeddings can be arbitrary, and for some regularized linear models it is not unique. The cause is a rescaling freedom in the embeddings, not cosine itself.
  number: none
  setup: Linear matrix factorization / linear autoencoder, X ≈ X A B^T, trained with Eq. 1 (L2 penalty on the product AB^T). Analytical result.
  quote: "We show that cosine similarity of the learned embeddings can in fact yield arbitrary results. We find that the underlying reason is not cosine similarity itself, but the fact that the learned embeddings have a degree of freedom that can render arbitrary cosine-similarities even though their (unnormalized) dot-products are well-defined and unique."
  where: p.2 (Introduction)
- claim: Objective 1 (penalty on AB^T, equivalent to denoising/dropout) is invariant to diagonal rescaling of the latent dimensions (A→AD, B→BD^-1). The dot-product model is unchanged, but the cosine similarities change with D. Objective 2 (separate penalties on XA and B, like weight decay) has no such freedom, so its cosine similarities are unique up to rotation.
  number: none
  setup: Eq. 1 vs Eq. 2. Cosine is invariant to rotation R, but not to D.
  quote: "the first (but not the second) objective is also invariant to rescalings of the columns of A and B (i.e., the different latent dimensions of the embeddings): if ˆA ˆB⊤ is a solution of the first objective, so is ˆADD−1 ˆB⊤ where D ∈ Rk×k is an arbitrary diagonal matrix."
  where: pp.3-4, Sec 2.1
- claim: Full-rank worked example. One choice of D makes item-item cosine similarity the identity matrix, so every item is similar only to itself. Another choice gives a nontrivial similarity. The same model gives very different similarities.
  number: cosSim(B,B) = V V^T = I
  setup: Eq. 1, full rank k = p, D = dMat(1/(1+λ/σi²))^(1/2). Analytical.
  quote: "which is quite a bizarre result, as it says that the cosine-similarity between any pair of (different) item-embeddings is zero, i.e., an item is only similar to itself, but not to any other item!"
  where: p.5, Sec 2.2
- claim: With that same D, user-item cosine gives exactly the same item ranking per user as the unnormalized dot-product. The row normalization is a constant per user. With the opposite D, user-user cosine reduces to similarities on the raw data matrix X, with no smoothing from the learned embeddings.
  number: none
  setup: Eq. 1, full rank.
  quote: "hence, when we consider the ranking of the items for a given user based on the predicted scores, cosine-similarity and (unnormalized) dot-product result in exactly the same ranking of the items"
  where: p.5
- claim: Objective 2 gives unique cosine similarities, but the authors leave open whether that unique scaling gives the best semantic similarity. They suggest D = dMat(sqrt(1/σi)) as the analogous choice for Objective 1.
  number: none
  setup: Closed form from Zheng et al. 2018, Eq. 6.
  quote: "While this solution is unique, it remains an open question if this unique diagonal matrix ... yields the best possible semantic similarities in practice."
  where: p.6, Sec 2.3
- claim: The three item-item cosine similarity patterns from rescaling under Eq. 1, and the one from Eq. 2, differ greatly from each other and from the ground-truth clusters. The authors only describe this qualitatively. No metric is given.
  number: n=20,000 users; p=1,000 items; C=5 clusters; rank k=50; λ=10,000 (Eq. 1) and λ=100 (Eq. 2); item powerlaw exponent βc ~ Unif(0.25, 1.5); user powerlaw β=0.5
  setup: Simulated cluster data with known ground truth. Low-rank (k=50 ≪ p=1,000). Cosine is applied to learned embeddings.
  quote: "we generated interactions between n = 20 , 000 users and p = 1, 000 items that were randomly assigned to C = 5 clusters" and "We used a low-rank constraint k = 50 ≪ p = 1, 000"
  where: pp.7-8, Sec 4 (results shown in Fig. 1)
- claim: Remedies. (a) Train directly with cosine, for example with layer normalization. (b) Project back to the original space and apply cosine to the rows of X A B^T. (c) Normalize or de-bias popularity before or during learning: standardize X, use negative sampling or inverse propensity scaling (IPS). word2vec samples negatives with frequency^(3/4).
  number: β = 3/4
  setup: Discussion only. Not tested experimentally.
  quote: "in word2vec [5], a matrix factorization model was trained by sampling negatives with a probability proportional to their frequency (popularity) in the training data taken to the power of β = 3/4"
  where: p.7, Sec 3
- claim: Normalization in cosine happens only after training. This can noticeably reduce the quality of the resulting semantic similarities compared with normalizing before or during learning.
  number: none
  setup: Argument, not measured.
  quote: "in cosine-similarity, normalization is applied only after the embeddings have been learned. This can noticeably reduce the resulting (semantic) similarities"
  where: p.7, Sec 3
- claim: Cosine sometimes beats the unnormalized dot-product and sometimes loses to it in practice. The paper cites DPR (Karpukhin 2020), ColBERT (Khattab 2020) and Zhou 2022 for the cases where it did worse.
  number: none
  setup: Cited from other work, not run here.
  quote: "it was, however, also found to not work as well as other approaches, like the (unnormalized) dot-product between the learned embeddings, e.g., see [3, 4, 8]."
  where: p.2
- claim: Objective 1 (the dropout-equivalent one) was found to give better held-out prediction accuracy than Objective 2. So the better-predicting model is the one with the arbitrary cosine.
  number: none
  setup: Cited from Jin et al. 2021 [2], not tested here.
  quote: "the resulting prediction accuracy on held-out test-data was experimentally found to be superior to the one of the second objective [2]."
  where: p.3

LIMITS
- Theory covers linear models only. The authors concede this: "this short paper is limited to linear models". They only "expect" deep models to have similar or larger problems. That is a conjecture.
- Experiments use simulated data only, and results are qualitative (heatmaps in Fig. 1). They have no real text embeddings, no retrieval benchmarks and no ANN or vector database experiments. The authors say they know of no good semantic similarity metric.
- The remedies are proposed but not tested. No quantitative comparison of cosine vs dot product vs the remedies.
- The setting is recommender-style MF (user-item). It does not examine pretrained LLM or text embedding models, contrastive training, or any retrieval index. Applying it to RAG embeddings is an extrapolation by the caller, not a claim of the paper.
- For a vector DB note: the paper does not discuss metric choice in indexes (cosine vs inner product vs L2), nor ANN. It supports a caution only: cosine is not automatically the "semantic" metric.
- It is a preprint, v1 only, 2024.

BUILDS ON: Jin et al. 2021 (KDD, closed form for Eq. 1 and the dropout equivalence); Steck 2020 (NeurIPS, "Autoencoders that don't overfit towards the identity", denoising/dropout equivalence); Zheng, Ding, Nie 2018 (arXiv:1804.05090, regularized SVD, closed form for Eq. 2); Ba et al. 2016 (layer normalization); Mikolov et al. 2013 (word2vec negative sampling); Karpukhin 2020 (DPR); Khattab and Zaharia 2020 (ColBERT); Zhou et al. 2022 (cosine problems for high-frequency words).

CODE: none in the paper. Key formulas, verbatim from the extraction:
- Eq. 1: min_{A,B} ||X − XAB⊤||²F + λ||AB⊤||²F (p.3)
- Eq. 2: min_{A,B} ||X − XAB⊤||²F + λ(||XA||²F + ||B||²F) (p.3)
- Eq. 3: Â(D) := ÂD and B̂(D) := B̂D^−1 (p.3)

FIGURES: Fig. 1 (p.7): "Illustration of the large variability of item-item cosine similarities cosSim(B, B) on the same data due to different modeling choices. Left: ground-truth clusters... the center three plots show three particular choices of re-scaling... Right: based on (unique) B obtained when training w.r.t. Eq. 2." It shows at a glance that one model gives very different similarity matrices. Image not viewed, caption only.

PROBLEMS: Extraction is text-only. Math is garbled (for example "11+λ/σ2i" stands for 1/(1+λ/σ_i²), and the subscripts and superscripts are misplaced). The quotes with equations are copied as extracted. No embedded instructions in the PDF. The system-reminder text in the tool result was not part of the PDF and was ignored.
